summary: Proposes a device-independent description of a graphical display, so graphics sent over the ARPANET can be turned into a picture on whatever device the receiving user has. It updates RFC 125 and mentions the form machine idea in RFC 94.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC proposes a common way to describe a graphical display for different devices. The receiving host interprets the description and adapts it to its own screen or output device.

questions: what is a device independent graphical display description
how can graphics be sent across the network
subtitle: A proposal for describing graphics so different display devices can render the same content.

tldr.problem: ARPANET hosts had different graphics displays, so graphical information needed a device-independent description.
tldr.mechanism: A graphics stream contains byte-coded commands and named lists that a receiving host interprets and converts for its display device.
tldr.outcome: The proposal updates RFC 125 and leaves much picture interaction unresolved. It was updated by RFC 181.

sections.title: A Device-Independent Graphics Description
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a standard description for sending graphical information between hosts with different display processors. The using host makes any conversions needed for its specific device. The proposal targets displays that can draw points, vectors and characters, but it also allows other display and hard-copy devices at the using host's discretion.

The document defines a graphics description stream (NGDS), interpreters, display lists, image areas, a screen, a list pointer and an execution stack.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal describes a picture in commands rather than for one specific display. The receiving host converts those commands for its own device.

sections.title: Screens, Coordinates and Display Lists
sections.content:
The network standard screen is rectangular. A position is an (x,y) pair of 16-bit unsigned fractions measured from the left and bottom edges. The format does not specify screen resolution, so a receiving device can render the same coordinates at its available resolution.

The screen may contain named rectangular image areas. The main image area is named 0 and covers the screen. Display lists contain commands for actions such as moving the beam, drawing a vector, displaying characters, calling another list, or changing the display mode.
sections.plainLanguage: The screen uses fractional coordinates, so the description does not depend on a particular display resolution. Named image areas and display lists organize the picture's parts and drawing commands.

sections.title: Commands and Picture Interaction
sections.content:
Commands use an eight-bit code followed by any required parameters. They can erase the screen, define lists or image areas, draw and display items, and translate, scale or rotate list instances. Unsupported enhanced modes are treated as no-ops by a device that cannot provide them.

The RFC says interaction with a displayed picture is not fully addressed. Keyboards and function keys can send messages, but associating a selected point with a meaningful part of the picture is harder. It distinguishes synchronous devices, such as light pens, from devices that can interact at any time, and defines different interaction information for each.
sections.plainLanguage: The commands describe how to draw and modify a picture. The RFC only sketches how a host should report user actions on the picture.
